queueStats.title: Job Queue

queue.events-ingest: Receives the alarms from the monitoring sources: normalises the payload, matches it to a CI and runs the correlation.
queue.events-correlate: Deferred correlation: takes up an alarm again when its delay expires, and the events suppressed by a change window when the window closes.
queue.events-maintenance: Every five minutes: closed change windows, pending alarms, flapping, storms to cool down and the event health gauges.
queue.services-impact: Recalculates the health of a monitored service when a CI of its map changes, and keeps the live maps aligned with the CMDB.
queue.service-impact-consumer: Listens to the CI health changes and to the end of an alarm storm, and queues the service maps to re-evaluate.
queue.notification-service: Delivers the notifications of a domain event on the configured channels: in-app, email, Slack and Teams.
queue.sla-engine: Starts, suspends and closes the SLA of a ticket following the events of its lifecycle.
queue.escalation-consumer: On an SLA or OLA breach, performs the escalation transition declared in the workflow.
queue.automation-consumer: Feeds AutoTriggers and business rules with the domain events: creation, update, field change, transition, SLA breach.
queue.workflow-jobs: The timed work of the workflow: step deadlines, OLA pass, automatic closure, webhook retries and trigger timers.
queue.notification-jobs: Deferred checks of a workflow: the escalation check and the wait of a timed step.
queue.sla-jobs: The SLA timers: one job per deadline, which makes the warning and the breach go off.
queue.email-digest: Sends the daily digest by email to each organisation at the time set in its notification rule.
queue.webhook-delivery: Calls the outbound webhooks, with retries and HMAC signature.
queue.report-scheduler: Runs the scheduled reports when their cron goes off, and delivers the result.
queue.anomaly-scanner: Goes through CIs and tickets looking for the anomalies declared by the rules.
queue.discovery-sync: Imports the CIs from the discovery sources and reconciles them with the CMDB.
queue.embeddings: Computes the embeddings of incidents and KB articles, which power the similar incidents and the suggested articles.
queue.maintenance: Nightly maintenance: database backup, purge of the resolved events and retention of the in-app notifications.
queue.autoanalisi: Self-analysis: dossier on GitHub and state of the analysis

queueStats.consumerNote: Domain consumer queues (notifications, SLA, escalation, service impact) cannot be retried from the UI: an exhausted event must be re-emitted by its producer.

keptHelp.failed: The failed jobs the queue keeps for diagnosis. They are removed after a while, and a retried job leaves this count as soon as it succeeds.

domainMatrices.title: Domain matrices
domainMatrices.subtitle: The rules that translate one vocabulary value into another: priority = impact × urgency, service criticality → impact, alarm severity → incident severity and CI health, change type × risk band, import severity, environment → change risk. They used to live in the code; here they change with no deploy.
domainMatrices.staleHint: These keys no longer match any value in your vocabularies: they are what a rename left behind. Saving the matrix removes them.

priority.title: Ticket priority
priority.description: Incident and problem priority = impact × urgency (ITIL). The derived priority is stored in the «severity» field, which SLA, badges and filters read.

service_impact.title: Service criticality → impact
service_impact.description: The impact of the incident a service map opens, from the criticality of the business application. The criticalities that translate to the highest impact are also the ones behind the «critical services down» banner.

event_severity.title: Alarm severity → incident severity
event_severity.description: The severity an incident opened by monitoring is born with. It also applies to an alarm-storm incident, which uses the highest alarm severity.

change_priority.title: Change priority
change_priority.description: Change priority = type × risk band (not impact × urgency). With the risk not yet assessed, the lowest band is used.

import_severity.title: Incoming severity from the import
import_severity.description: How the severities written in a ticket import file are translated. A severity that cannot be translated puts the row in error: it is no longer rewritten to «medium».

change_priority_initial.title: Initial change priority
change_priority_initial.description: The priority a change is born with before its risk has been assessed: from the change type alone. Once the assessment produces a score, «type × risk band» takes over.

environment_risk.title: Environment → change risk
environment_risk.description: How much the environment of a CI adds to the risk score of its change assessment, from 0 (nothing) to 3 (the most). An environment with no value stops the assessment and says so.

ci_health.title: Alarm severity → CI health
ci_health.description: The health a firing alarm gives its CI: operational, degraded or down. Among several firing alarms the worst health wins; a flapping alarm always counts as degraded. A severity with no value stops the health update and says so.

service_urgency.title: Service health → incident urgency
service_urgency.description: The urgency of the incident that Monitored services open when a service goes down or degraded. Together with the impact from the application criticality it gives the priority. A health with no value stops the incident from opening and says so.

major_incident_priority.title: Major incident → priority
major_incident_priority.description: The priority an incident takes when it is declared a Major Incident; its SLA follows the new priority. Revoking the declaration does not lower it. With no value, the declaration stops and says so.

domainMatrices.missingWarning_one: One combination with no value ({{keys}}). While it stays empty, the operation that needs it — opening an incident, or an incoming alarm — stops and says so: fill it in here.
domainMatrices.missingWarning_other: {{count}} combinations with no value ({{keys}}). While they stay empty, the operation that needs them — opening an incident, or an incoming alarm — stops and says so: fill them in here.
domainMatrices.invalidWarning_one: One cell points at a value that is no longer in your vocabulary ({{keys}}): it is what a rename left behind, and at runtime it is an error. Pick the new value.
domainMatrices.invalidWarning_other: {{count}} cells point at values that are no longer in your vocabulary ({{keys}}): they are what a rename left behind, and at runtime they are errors. Pick the new values.

The thresholds used to be hardcoded (30 and 60) and the bands were read by position in the vocabulary: reordering it silently inverted them, and a fourth band never fired even though it appeared in the matrix.

It is the only feature whose proposals, once accepted, let the model write text that people will read: the labels of your values. enum.emptyValues: Dictionary "{{name}}" has {{count}} empty values: every value needs a name.
enum.systemTenant: The system tenant does not customize the shipped dictionaries: the product changes those.
enum.renameEmpty: The new value cannot be empty.
enum.noValues: Dictionary "{{name}}" cannot be left without values: no record could be created any more, because every value would be rejected as out of vocabulary. If it is no longer needed, delete it; if you are rewriting the scale, send it whole.
enum.duplicateValues: Dictionary "{{name}}" repeats {{values}}: in a scale the position is a domain rule (the first value is the lowest, the last the highest), and a repeated value makes it ambiguous.
enum.unknownLanguage: Language "{{language}}" not recognised: the product is translated into {{available}}.
enum.alreadyYours: Dictionary "{{name}}" is already yours: edit it directly, there is nothing to customize.
enum.yoursExists: You already have a dictionary "{{name}}": that is the one you read. Edit it instead of creating another.
enum.shippedUseCustomize: Dictionary "{{name}}" ships with the product: it is the same for every tenant and cannot be edited in place. Use "Customize" to get your own copy and edit that.
enum.replacementNotRemoved: Replacements: "{{from}}" is not among the values you are removing from "{{name}}" ({{removed}}).
enum.replacementNothingRemoved: Replacements: "{{from}}" is not among the values you are removing from "{{name}}", and you are removing none.
enum.replacementNotNew: Replacements: the replacement value "{{to}}" is not among the new values of "{{name}}" ({{values}}).
enum.removingDefault: You are removing "{{value}}" from "{{name}}", which is its default value: a new record would be born with a value the dictionary does not have. Say what to rewrite it to, or choose a new default in the same operation.
enum.defaultNotInValues: The default value "{{value}}" is not among the values of "{{name}}" ({{values}}).
enum.deleteInUse: Deleting your dictionary "{{name}}" would bring it back to the one shipped with the product ({{shipped}}), and these values of yours are still in use: {{usages}}. Change those records first, or remove the values one by one with a replacement value.
enum.deleteInUseNoShipped: Deleting your dictionary "{{name}}" would leave no value at all (there is no shipped one), and these values are still in use: {{usages}}. Change those records first.
enum.shippedRename: Dictionary "{{name}}" ships with the product: it is the same for every tenant and cannot be edited in place. Use "Customize" to get your own copy, and rename the values on that one.
enum.renameMissing: Value "{{from}}" is not among those of "{{name}}" ({{values}}): there is nothing to rename.
enum.renameWouldMerge: "{{name}}" already has a value "{{to}}". Renaming "{{from}}" to "{{to}}" would merge two distinct values into one, and the records of the first would become the second without anyone asking. If that is what you want, remove "{{from}}" giving "{{to}}" as its replacement.
enum.shippedReorder: Dictionary "{{name}}" ships with the product: use "Customize" to get your own copy and reorder that one.
enum.reorderSameSet: Reordering changes only the ORDER of the values of "{{name}}", not the set (missing: {{missing}} · extra: {{extra}}). To add or remove a value use the dictionary edit, to change its name use the rename.
enum.otherTenant: Dictionary "{{name}}" belongs to another tenant: it cannot be attached to field "{{field}}".
enum.sharedFieldOwnDictionary: Field "{{field}}" ships with the product and is shared by every tenant: it cannot be attached to your dictionary "{{name}}", because your values would end up in the other tenants too. Create a dictionary named "{{name}}" — yours wins on read only for you.

enum.unknownValueColor: «{{color}}» is not one of the available colors ({{available}}).

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.threshold: an alarm opens an incident only if its severity is at least the one chosen in “Open incident from”; below the threshold it stays in the console without an incident.
howItWorks.grouping: later alarms attach to the incident already open for the same CI (or the same fingerprint); the open delay absorbs short spikes.
howItWorks.autoResolve: when the source resolves every alarm, the incident opened by monitoring is resolved; if the alarm comes back, it is reopened.
howItWorks.changeWindow: alarms on the CIs of a change in its release window are suppressed: no incident, no health change; at the end of the window they are re-evaluated.
howItWorks.lifecycle: alarms on CIs in the chosen lifecycle statuses (usually “decommissioned”) open no incident and do not change the health: the alarm stays in the console with its reason.
howItWorks.flapping: an alarm that comes and goes too many times within the window is marked “flapping”: no incident opened or closed, CI health degraded, until it stays stable for the given minutes.
howItWorks.storm: if a source sends more new alarms per minute than the threshold, they are all grouped into a single storm incident instead of one per CI, until the rate stays below the threshold for the given minutes.

help.openIncidentFrom: Minimum severity from which an alarm opens an incident. “Never” = alarms stay in the console only.
help.groupBy: CI: one incident per CI, all its alarms attached. Fingerprint: one incident per distinct alarm.
help.openDelaySeconds: Seconds to wait before opening: if the alarm resolves within the delay, no incident. 0 = open immediately.
help.suppressUpstreamHops: How far up the dependency chain to look for a change in its window: 0 = only the alarm's CI; 1 = also a CI it directly depends on (e.g. a database being released silences alarms of the application that uses it).
help.flapThreshold: Above this number of firing/resolved transitions within the window the alarm is marked “flapping” and opens no new incident.
help.flapWindowMinutes: Observation window in which flapping transitions are counted.
help.retentionDays: Resolved events older than this many days are deleted.
help.matchShortHostname: If the alarm resource is an FQDN (db-01.example.local) also try the short name (db-01), and vice versa. Off: exact name or alias only. Beware of identical short names across environments.
help.autoResolve: When the source resolves every alarm of an incident opened by monitoring, the incident is resolved; a new alarm reopens it.
help.severityMap: Impact and urgency assigned to the automatically opened incident, from the alarm severity: the priority derives from them.
help.flapStableMinutes: How long the alarm must stay still (no new firing or resolved) before leaving the flapping state and returning to normal correlation.
help.stormThresholdPerMinute: When a source exceeds this number of new alarms per minute, a storm starts: its alarms are grouped into a single incident instead of opening one per CI. 0 = storm detection off.
help.stormCooldownMinutes: The storm ends once the rate stays below the threshold for this many minutes; later alarms return to normal correlation.
help.ignoreLifecycleStatuses: Alarms on CIs in these statuses open no incident and do not change the CI health: they stay in the console with the reason “lifecycle ignored”. “decommissioned” is usually enough: a retired CI the monitoring has not switched off yet must wake nobody.
help.retiredStatuses: A CI in these statuses does not count in the service health: it shows on the map, marked “retired”, but carries no weight and never puts the service under maintenance. Shipped default: “inactive” and “decommissioned”.
help.maintenanceStatuses: A CI in these statuses is not updated by monitoring and leaves the map calculation, marked “under maintenance”. This is the CI lifecycle, not a change window. Shipped default: “maintenance”.
help.highImpactDependents: From how many dependent CIs upwards the console marks a CI as «a failure here spreads». 0 = no emphasis, only the count is shown.
help.productionEnvironments: The values of the environment vocabulary that count as production. A CI without an environment counts as production.
help.nonProductionSeverityMap: Off: the table above applies everywhere. On: the CIs outside production use their own table.
